title: Start here: how Learn works
summary: A five-minute tour. One small problem shows every tool: colored parts, cards you can drill into, steps with reasons, live graphs, proofs, @ references and sharing.

d.label: $d$
d.body: Written in the problem as a number. Units: km.
d.example: Bangkok to Ayutthaya by road is about 80 km.
d.analogy: The length of the rope you have to walk along.

t1.label: $t_1$
t1.body: Only the time the train is rolling. It does **not** include the stop.

t2.label: $t_2$
t2.body: Easy to forget. The words *for the whole trip* say it must be counted. This is a {hidden_given|hidden given}.
t2.analogy: Time on the clock keeps running while you wait at the station.

tt.label: $T$
tt.meaning: total time of the trip: 2 h
tt.body: Not asked for, but it is the bridge to the answer: $\p{tt}{T} = \p{t1}{t_1} + \p{t2}{t_2}$.

v.label: $\bar v$
v.meaning: average speed for the whole trip
v.body: What the question asks. Units: km/h. Defined by the {avg_speed|average speed formula}.

whole.label: whole trip
whole.meaning: the time to use is all of it, stops included
whole.body: Two small words that change the answer from 80 km/h to 60 km/h.

hidden_given.title: Hidden given
hidden_given.body: Information the problem gives you in **words**, not as a number. Spotting it is a core skill. Here it is [t2:the stop] together with [whole:whole trip]. In physics, *starts from rest* is a classic one: it means $v_0 = 0$.
hidden_given.analogy: A shop sign that says *open daily* also tells you it is open on Sunday.

mean_trap.title: Averaging speeds is a trap
mean_trap.body: The plain mean of two speeds is **not** the average speed, unless you spend the same **time** at each speed. The proof section shows a counterexample line by line.
mean_trap.useWhen: you are tempted to add speeds and divide by 2.

merton.title: The Merton scholars
merton.body: In the 1330s a group at Merton College, Oxford studied *uniformly changing* motion and proved the {mean_speed|mean speed theorem}. They worked in words and proportions, long before algebra notation existed.

f_part.title: Parts (colored pieces)
f_part.body: A part is one thing in the lesson: a quantity, an actor, a condition. It has **one color for the whole lesson**. Hover it anywhere (text, formula, graph, slider) and it lights up everywhere, while the rest dims. The badge says its role: given, {hidden_given|hidden given}, derived, goal…
f_part.example: Hover [v:$\bar v$] now, then look at the plot further down.
f_part.analogy: Highlighter pens: one color per character in a novel.

f_card.title: Cards and drill-down
f_card.body: Dashed words open a card in the side panel. Hover to preview, **click to pin**. Inside a pinned card, dashed words open the next level. A breadcrumb and a *where this sits* tree show the path you took, so you can climb back up. Try {avg_speed|average speed} → {total_time|total time}.
f_card.analogy: Wikipedia links, but the trail is always visible and you never lose your place.

f_concept.title: Shared concepts
f_concept.body: Some cards are **shared concepts**: written once and reused by every lesson that needs them, such as {avg_speed|average speed} here or Newton's laws in physics. They carry a *shared concept* badge and show how many lessons use them. Their prerequisites appear in the drill-down tree, so you can always go one level deeper.
f_concept.analogy: A shared dictionary: every book links to the same entry instead of writing its own.

f_chain.title: Chain of steps
f_chain.body: Solutions and explanations come as numbered steps. Each step has a **move** (what we do), a **why** (which rule allows it) and often a **why not** (why the other option fails). Hover a step and only the parts it uses stay lit.

f_try.title: Show me / Let me try
f_try.body: The switch at the top. In *let me try* mode, formulas, answers and reasons are blurred until you click them. Say your answer first, then reveal. Answering before reading is what makes it stick.

f_widget.title: Live visuals
f_widget.body: Graphs, diagrams and flows are drawn from the lesson's data, not pasted as images. Sliders change the numbers and every linked part updates. Lessons can only use the built-in widgets, so a shared lesson can never run its own code.
f_widget.example: Drag the stop-time slider in the plot and watch [v:$\bar v$] fall.

f_graph.title: Concept graph
f_graph.body: Shows what each idea is built from. Arrows point from what is needed to what uses it. Hover a node to light up everything it depends on: that is your list of prerequisites.

f_proof.title: Line-by-line proofs
f_proof.body: Each proof line has a claim, the reason it holds, and sometimes the intuition. Hover a line to see which earlier lines it uses. For maths, this is where most of the learning happens.

f_ref.title: @ references
f_ref.body: Every piece of a lesson has an address, like `@guide/chain.s2`. **Alt-click** anything, press **@** while hovering, or use *@ add* on a pinned card. It becomes a chip in the ask bar. Your question plus the exact pieces you pointed at go to pi together, so you never have to explain which step you mean.
f_ref.example: `@guide/chain.s2` = step 2 of the chain in this guide.

f_recall.title: Recall
f_recall.body: A few questions at the end, answered from memory. All options have similar length and form, so the shape of an answer never gives it away.

f_lang.title: English and Thai
f_lang.body: Switch the language at the top. A lesson and its translation share the same parts, cards and step addresses, so a `@` reference or a comment points at the same thing in both languages.

f_community.title: Share with the community
f_community.body: Lessons start **private** in your library. You can make one *unlisted* (anyone with the link) or *public* (listed in Explore). A public lesson needs one {category|category} and 1–5 {tag|tags}. Others can like, comment on any step, and {fork|fork} it.

category.title: Category
category.body: Where a lesson lives, from a fixed tree, e.g. *math › analysis › real analysis*. Exactly one per lesson. Browse Explore by category to find a subject.

tag.title: Tag
tag.body: A free label such as `friction`, `epsilon-delta` or `unit-economics`. One to five per lesson. Tags cut across categories: `proof-by-contradiction` can appear in algebra and in analysis.

fork.title: Fork
fork.body: Copy someone's lesson into your library to study or change it. The original author stays credited. Forking is free and instant, so search before you create.

f_pi.title: pi, your tutor
f_pi.body: Lessons are written by **pi**, an AI tutor that runs on your computer. Ask it a question, a problem, or a topic to learn. It writes the lesson in this format and publishes it here with `/publish`. Creating lessons from the website is coming next.

sections.title: Welcome
sections.body:
Learn turns a question into a lesson you can **explore**, not just read. Every lesson is split into small pieces you can hover, click and point at.

This guide is itself a lesson. It walks through one small problem and stops at each tool on the way. Look for the dashed words and colored pieces, and keep the side panel open: that is where cards appear.

Two things to try right now: hover [d:$d$], then click {f_part|parts} to pin its card.

sections.note: click any name to open its card

What to do

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: A train covers [d:a distance of 120 km] in [t1:1.5 hours of travel]. On the way it [t2:stops at a station for 30 minutes]. What is its [v:average speed] for the [whole:whole trip]?

sections.title: Chunks
sections.note: the problem, split into pieces with a role

rows.note: $t_2 = 0.5$ h. Easy to skip: see {hidden_given|hidden given}

sections.title: Concept → Field
sections.concept: Average speed compares **distance** with **time** over a whole interval. The only subtle point is which time to use.
sections.field: Kinematics, the description of motion. Needed first: {avg_speed|average speed} and {total_time|total time}.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: two routes people take; one is wrong

routes.title: Route A
routes.why: the question says [whole:whole trip], and the definition of average speed uses total time.

routes.title: Route B
routes.why: it gives the speed **while moving** (80 km/h), which is a real number about the trip.
routes.whyNot: it ignores [t2:the stop], so it answers a different question. See {mean_trap|the trap}.

sections.notUsed: Not used: acceleration formulas. Nothing in the problem says how the speed changes, and we don't need to know.

sections.title: Chain
sections.note: hover a step to see which parts it uses

steps.why: the [whole:whole trip] includes the stop, so both times count. See {total_time|total time}.
steps.whyNot: using only [t1:$t_1$] would leave out half an hour the clock really ran.

steps.why: definition of average speed: total distance over total time.
80 km/h is the moving speed. The stop pulls the average down, so 60 < 80 makes sense.

sections.title: See it
sections.note: drag the sliders; the average speed is the slope of the straight line

sections.title: Check
items: **No stop**: with [t2:$t_2$] = 0 the average equals the moving speed, 80 km/h ✓ (set the slider to 0)
**Size**: 60 km/h is below the moving speed 80 km/h, as it must be when the train waits ✓

sections.title: What it is built from
sections.note: arrows point from what is needed to what uses it; hover a node

sections.title: The trap, proved
sections.note: hover a line to see which lines it uses
sections.goal: The mean of two speeds is not, in general, the {avg_speed|average speed}.

lines.claim: Take a trip of 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 90 km/h.
lines.why: one example where the claim fails is enough to show it is not always true.
lines.intuition: pick two very different speeds so the effect is big.

lines.why: time = distance ÷ speed for each part.
{avg_speed|average speed}: total distance over total time.

lines.intuition: the slow part takes **longer**, so it counts more in the true average.
lines.whyNot: the two agree only if equal **times** are spent at each speed.

events.text: {merton|The Merton scholars} in Oxford state the {mean_speed|mean speed theorem} for steadily changing motion.
Nicole Oresme draws speed against time and reads distance as an **area**, an early graph like the plot above.
Galileo uses the same result in *Two New Sciences* to describe falling bodies.

sections.title: Sharing and the community
sections.body:
Everything you make starts in your library. When a lesson is ready, {f_community|share it}: pick a {category|category}, add a few {tag|tags}, and choose *public* or *unlisted*.

In Explore you can browse by category, filter by tag and lesson type, and search. If a lesson already covers your question, {fork|fork} it instead of starting over. Comments attach to a specific step or proof line, using the same addresses as {f_ref|@ references}.

sections.title: Making lessons
sections.body:
Lessons are written by {f_pi|pi}, an AI tutor on your computer. Give it a problem to solve, a topic to learn (it makes a study plan first), a business situation, or a programming idea. It writes the lesson in this format, and `/publish` puts it in your library here.

Creating lessons directly on the website is **in progress**. This guide will tell you when it arrives.

The guide works the same in {f_lang|English and Thai}.

sections.title: Recall
sections.note: answer from memory before you click

questions.q: The train stops for 1 hour instead of 30 minutes. What is $\bar v$?
How do you put one exact step into your question for pi?
questions.why: Alt-click (or @ while hovering) adds an @ reference, so pi gets the exact step and its formulas.

questions.q: Which words in the problem hide a given?
questions.why: *whole trip* means the stop time counts. That is a hidden given.
